$schema-note: Hand-written, machine-swept. Data, not code: nothing under src/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for WIN-267 T4 (M4.1) — serving the one-time-secret mints
carrying the file it lives in (repository-relative), the EXACT text that
implements it (`from`), the edit that removes it (`to`), the suites run, and
the NAMED cases that were SEEN to go red (`kills`).
`kills` IS OBSERVED, NOT INTENDED. `mutation-sweep.mjs` applies each entry,
runs the named suites through vitest's JSON reporter, records the failing
case titles and restores the file. An entry whose whole suite goes red is
reported VACUOUS — a module-load failure proves nothing about any single
guard — and an entry nothing kills is reported SURVIVED. Both are defects in
SEPARATE FROM mutations-win267-t3.json, which is the adapter-construction
ledger. Appending here would have made one file whose entries only make
sense read against two different dimensions.
procedure: Suites, by the key each entry names:
NONE of these entries needs a database, a container or a network. The mint's
three contracts are doubles in the `mint` suite by design — what a double
can witness is which method was called and with what — and the `route` suite
reads decorator metadata and two committed files off disk. Whether the vault
actually advances a revision in PostgreSQL is that context's own integration
suite's claim and is NOT re-asserted here.

sweep.head: the tree of the commit that carries this file, on tejas/win-267-t4-mints (base v1 @ 007007f2)

mutations.name: T01 the mint asks for a WEAKER access level, so a read-only operator may rotate a live secret
mutations.note: The headline privilege defect. Nothing about the response shape changes, every status assertion still passes, and the operation becomes callable by an operator with read-only access. Killed by the case that reads the ARGUMENT the tenancy double recorded.
kills: the channel webhook-secret mint the authorization gate asks for secret:mutate and not for a weaker level

mutations.name: T02 the caller is handed a DIFFERENT secret from the one sealed in the vault
mutations.note: The defect worth the most and the cheapest to introduce: every caller gets a live-looking secret that authenticates nothing, and no status code or shape assertion can see it. Killed by reading the sealed value back out of the command the vault was handed.
kills: the channel webhook-secret mint the rotation mints one secret and hands the caller the same bytes it sealed

mutations.name: T03 the minted secret is quietly narrowed below the width the frozen oracle mints
mutations.note: A security regression invisible in a diff. The case that kills it reads `randomBytes(N)` off `apps/agent/src/agent-runtime/channels.controller.ts` — a file this dimension does not control — precisely so that narrowing the constant cannot move both sides of the assertion.
kills: the channel webhook-secret mint the rotation mints exactly as wide a secret as the FROZEN ORACLE mints

mutations.name: T04 an END_USER credential may mint an operator's secret
mutations.note: The tier gate. `identity-access` answers who the caller is; requiring OPERATOR is this operation's own rule, so removing it is invisible to that context's suites.
kills: the channel webhook-secret mint the identity gate refuses an END_USER credential

mutations.name: T05 an ORGANIZATION-scoped credential is treated as naming an environment vault
mutations.note: Deleting the `null` check outright is a COMPILE ERROR, not a defect — `environmentId` would stop satisfying the tenancy call's parameter — so the mutation that models the real hazard is one level up: widen the resolver so an organization-scoped bearer yields an id the vault will happily be keyed by. That is a genuine cross-tenant reach and it type-checks.
kills: the channel webhook-secret mint the identity gate refuses a credential addressed above one environment

mutations.name: T06 the vault rotates whatever credential happens to be FIRST, not the one this channel names
mutations.note: A cross-tenant rotation primitive: one channel's rotate call destroys another channel's live webhook secret. Killed by the case that hands the listing a credential under a DIFFERENT name and expects a refusal.
kills: the channel webhook-secret mint finding the credential looks for the name channelWebhookCredentialName builds

mutations.name: T07 an empty secret is sealed instead of refused, defeating WIN-259's write-only guard
mutations.note: Deleting the `!held.ok` branch is a COMPILE ERROR — `held.value` is only present on the ok arm — so the mutation that models the real hazard is the one that makes the guard unreachable by substituting a value it accepts. A generator that failed would then seal a one-character secret instead of refusing, which is the exact outcome WIN-259's write-only guard exists to prevent.
kills: the channel webhook-secret mint the rotation refuses an empty minted secret rather than sealing one

mutations.name: T08 the three uncomposed-context refusals collapse into ONE name, so an operator cannot tell them apart
mutations.note: The fifth lesson this programme paid for — two guards returning the same value cannot be told apart. Three different repairs (wire an adapter, fix the caller, create the credential) hide behind one message.
kills: the channel webhook-secret mint refuses before it reaches a context it does not have names tenancy when tenancy is uncomposed

mutations.name: T09 the 404 echoes the attacker-controlled path parameter back into the log and onto the wire
mutations.from: message: "This channel connection has no webhook credential to rotate.",
mutations.to: message: `Channel ${_channelConnectionId} has no webhook credential to rotate.`,
mutations.note: The log-forging primitive `transport-errors.ts` refuses to build. Killed by the case that sends a marker id and asserts it appears nowhere in the serialised refusal.
kills: the channel webhook-secret mint finding the credential does NOT echo the channel connection id back in the refusal

mutations.name: T10 the route loses its version segment and stops being the operation the policy binds
mutations.note: The route would answer at `/api/v1/...` anyway via `defaultVersion`, so nothing about the process visibly breaks — but the mounted template reconstructed from the decorators no longer matches the policy's, which is exactly the drift the join exists to catch.
kills: the secret-mint controller's mounted routes carries the version segment, so `api/v1` appears in NO source literal
the secret-mint controller's mounted routes serves a template the idempotency policy classes `required`
the secret-mint controller's mounted routes is classified `required` by the gate's own matcher on a CONCRETE path
the secret-mint controller's mounted routes serves an operation the FROZEN SURFACE'S generated manifest already has

mutations.name: T11 the controller is mounted one segment off, so the gate reserves keys for an operation nothing serves
mutations.note: The failure every behavioural test in the suite is blind to: the handler works perfectly and is unreachable. Killed by both joins — the policy has no such template and neither does the frozen surface's generated manifest.
kills: the secret-mint controller's mounted routes serves a template the idempotency policy classes `required`
the secret-mint controller's mounted routes is classified `required` by the gate's own matcher on a CONCRETE path
the secret-mint controller's mounted routes serves an operation the FROZEN SURFACE'S generated manifest already has

mutations.name: T12 the mint's template is DEMOTED in the policy, so the gate stops requiring a key on it
mutations.note: The mint would still work and would still hand back a secret — it would simply no longer be protected against being run twice on a retry, which is the entire contract. Killed by the route join and by the policy suite's own reconciliation against the manifest.
